questions.question: Describe the Solar System, and explain why the Moon shines.
questions.expected_answer: The Sun, a star of hot, glowing gas, is at the centre, and its gravity keeps eight planets in orbit: the rocky inner planets Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, and the gas giants Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The asteroid belt, made of millions of rocky lumps, lies between Mars and Jupiter. The Moon does not make its own light; it shines because it reflects sunlight. Its surface has craters, mountains and plains.

questions.question: Explain the difference between rotation and revolution, and describe the movements of the Moon.
questions.expected_answer: Rotation is spinning on an axis: the Earth rotates in about twenty-four hours, which causes day and night. Revolution is travelling around another object: the Earth revolves around the Sun in 365¼ days, which is a year. The Moon revolves around the Earth in about a month and rotates once in about twenty-eight days, so the same side always faces us. The Earth and the Moon revolve around the Sun together.

questions.question: Describe one telescope in South Africa and one rover, and explain how each is designed to do its job.
questions.expected_answer: SALT, near Sutherland, is the largest single light telescope in the southern half of the world; its mirror of ninety-one pieces collects light from extremely faint objects, and it was built where the sky is high, dry and dark. Alternatively, MeerKAT near Carnarvon has sixty-four dishes that collect radio waves in a radio quiet zone. The Moon buggy used batteries because there is no air for petrol, wire-mesh wheels that could not go flat, and folded to fit on the lander. Mars rovers are robots with six wheels, cameras, arms with tools and solar or nuclear power, because signals take minutes to reach them.
